title: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment
plain_summary: Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.

experiment_conditions.fuel_or_material: PMMA rods (0.25, 0.375, 0.5 in, black and clear), PMMA sheets, SIBAL fabric
experiment_conditions.flow: Wind-tunnel max stated as 40 cm/s on p.3 and 0-55 cm/s on p.7 of the same file - UNRESOLVED
experiment_conditions.oxygen: 13.6% O2 steady spreading for 1/4-in PMMA rod in microgravity vs 16% O2 1g blowoff (p.18); MIST sub-test range 16-21% O2, 0.4-4 cm/s (p.14)
experiment_conditions.pressure: 1 atm in the SIBAL case on p.21 (18.7% O2)

reported_findings: Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s.
Three different diameters (0.25", 0.375", 0.5") of black and clear PMMA rods were tested.
Oxygen concentrations between 16% to 21% and flow velocity between 0.4 cm/sec to 4 cm/sec were tested.
The 1g blowoff for the ¼” rod is at 16% oxygen, whereas we obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen in BASS-II.
Thus the material has a negative Oxygen Margin of Safety of 2.4% O2, and the normal gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.
Examine how thermal and species fields can diverge and lead to microgravity flame extinguishment by varying fuel thickness.
Ignited at 5 cm/s flow at right end, then reduced to 2.2 cm/s gradually.

title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment
plain_summary: Preliminary results are presented for one test of the last flight of the Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire VI) which was conducted on an orbiting Cygnus spacecraft.

experiment_conditions.fuel_or_material: SIBAL cotton/fiberglass 50 cm long, 41 cm wide; two-sided PMMA 1 cm; one-sided PMMA 0.5 cm; Nomex 7 cm (did not ignite)
experiment_conditions.oxygen_pressure: VI-2 SIBAL 31.0% O2 / 54.1 kPa; VI-3 two-sided PMMA 30.3% / 54.6 kPa; VI-4 one-sided PMMA 28.8% / 55.2 kPa

reported_findings: Preliminary results are presented for one test of the last flight of the Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire VI) which was conducted on an orbiting Cygnus spacecraft.
The final flight in the series of six experiments examined concurrent spread over large samples (all 41 cm wide) including a thin sheet of flammable fuel (cotton/fiberglass 50 cm long)
Overall, the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were found to be less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.
The Nomex sample did not ignite and so it will not be included in this paper.
The smoke from the fire event was readily detected by an ionization detector and a light scattering system but a typical alarm threshold was only achieved at 981 seconds.
As can be seen in Table 2, the allowable CO2 level was exceeded by both of the PMMA tests on Saffire VI.
Practical scale fires ranging from 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in unmanned spacecraft with free air volumes of 17 to 19 cubic meters.
The SIBAL sample (left image) achieved a steady size and spread rate quite rapidly where the two PMMA samples grew continuously until the flow speed was reduced.

title: Laminar smoke points of coflowing flames in microgravity
plain_summary: Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in coflowing air.

experiment_conditions.fuel_or_material: Gas-jet diffusion flames: ethylene, propane, propylene, propylene/nitrogen mixtures
experiment_conditions.oxygen: ISS cabin air estimated 20-23% O2 in this paper

reported_findings: Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in coflowing air.
Microgravity was obtained on board the International Space Station.
A total of 55 smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures.
Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm, and coflow velocities varied from 5.4 to 65 cm/s.
The Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) was operated in the Microgravity Science Glovebox on board the International Space Station (ISS) in 2009.
The oxygen mole fraction of ISS cabin air was maintained within an estimated range of 20-23%.
The flames generally reached steady conditions within 10 s of ignition, or within 5 s of a change in fuel or air flow rate.
Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth orbit.

title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE)
plain_summary: SPICE will determine the laminar smoke point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations.

experiment_conditions.fuel_or_material: Gas-jet flames: propylene, propane, ethylene mixtures
experiment_conditions.flow: Nozzle diameter / co-flow configurations (summary only, no per-test table in this 2-page PDF)

reported_findings: SPICE will determine the laminar smoke point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations.
The smoke point is a simple measurement that has been found useful to study the influence of flow and fuel properties on the sooting propensity of flames.

The Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) determines the point at which gas-jet flames (similar to a butane-lighter flame) begin to emit soot (dark carbonaceous particulate formed inside the flame) in microgravity.
This investigation completed 250 combustion tests with various fuel mixtures, including propylene, propane, and ethylene, in microgravity.
Researchers identified more than 70 smoke points, which yielded estimates of soot-forming conditions and flame dimensions.

title: Extinction of solid diffusion flame in microgravity: details of quenching and blowoff processes
plain_summary: Long duration microgravity experiments aboard the International Space Station determine diffusion flame extinction limits of PMMA spheres.
reported_findings: Long duration microgravity experiments aboard the International Space Station determine diffusion flame extinction limits of PMMA spheres.

Upon ignition from an electrically-heated coil, the 4-cm-diameter samples are exposed to forced flows ranging from 0.2 to 80 cm/s and an oxygen ranging from 13 to 28% in one atmosphere total pressure.
Extinction is reached as oxygen concentration gradually decreases by natural depletion.
Quenching at low velocity is observed with the flame tip shrinking upstream and blowoff is observed when a hole forms in the flame at the forward flow stagnation point.
Five tests are presented as listed in Table 1.
In quenching, the flame tip shrinks toward the upstream, in blowoff, the flame base retreats toward the downstream.
Quenching starts with the flame tip shrinking toward the stagnation region.
This is the first report on the experimental findings from a recent microgravity experiment aboard the International Space Station studying the burning of a 4-cm diameter PMMA sphere.

title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) - Final Report
plain_summary: Four materials, typical of those found in spacecraft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, silicone rubber, and Teflon.

experiment_conditions.platform: ISS, Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), Expedition 15, Sep-early Oct 2007
experiment_conditions.fuel_or_material: Cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, silicone rubber, Teflon, dibutyl-phthalate on porous wick; heated below ignition, not burned

experiment_conditions.oxygen: Not a combustion test - materials heated below ignition

reported_findings: Four materials, typical of those found in spacecraft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, silicone rubber, and Teflon.
The transport time from the smoke source to the detector was simulated by holding the smoke in an aging chamber for times ranging from 10 seconds to 1800 seconds.
Therefore, a new procedure was developed, the moment method, from which the characteristics of the particle size distribution can be inferred using a minimum number of portable instrument.
The experimental results show that, for the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter.
The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity.
These were comprised of six samples each of 5 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, silicone rubber, cellulose, and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick.
Results from the moment instruments for baseline runs (no aging) and 720 second aging runs are summarized in Table 1.

title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity
plain_summary: The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.

experiment_conditions.fuel_or_material: Methanol droplets, 1.5-4 mm (1.5-4.5 mm in results text)
experiment_conditions.flow: Droplet combustion, no forced flow stated in abstract
experiment_conditions.oxygen: LOI around 12-13% O2 by volume; tests at 0.7 and 1 atm, O2 30% down to 12%, CO2/He diluents 0-70%

reported_findings: The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.

The initial droplet size varied between approximately 1.5 mm and 4 mm to capture both diffusive extinction brought about by insufficient residence time at the flame and radiative extinction caused by excessive heat loss from the flame zone.
More than 100 droplets have been burned.
Over one hundred methanol droplet tests in varying diluent concentrations and at primarily two different ambient pressures (0.7 and 1 atm) have been performed to date.

Considering the number of independent parameters involved, namely different initial droplet diameters, various oxygen and diluent concentrations, the simplified theoretical model predicts the flame-standoff ratio reasonably well.
This figure contains over 100 data points, covering a range of oxygen concentration, CO2 and He diluent concentrations, and initial droplet sizes, at two different pressure.

title: Detailed Results From the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011
plain_summary: It also presents the results of the first 284 tests performed.

experiment_conditions.platform: ISS, CIR / Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), Mar 2009-Dec 2011
experiment_conditions.oxygen: LOI objective; most tests 0.7-1 atm, many in air; observed LOI slightly lower than initially expected (no single LOI value stated in executive summary)

reported_findings: It also presents the results of the first 284 tests performed.
The intent is not to interpret the experimental results but rather to make them available to the entire scientific community for possible future interpretations.
The fuels studied in these experiments were methanol and n-heptane.
Most of the tests were conducted at pressures between 0.7 and 1 atm, and many of the tests were in air.
A principle objective was to determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI), the oxygen percentage below which combustion would not occur.
Both radiative and diffusive extinctions occurred during the testing.
Observed LOI values for these fuels appear to be slightly lower than initially expected.
